$comment: The tunables, declared once. Two stacks read this file — the Node services through libs/common/src/settings.ts and the Python admin through apps/admin/registry.py — so a knob is added here and appears in both, with the same bounds and the same default. It is data rather than code precisely because neither stack should own it.

groups.label: Sync cadence
groups.about: How often a wallet is rescanned. This is the top of the funnel: everything below it only decides how the work already asked for gets done.

groups.label: Throughput
groups.about: How fast the work is handed out once it is due. Turning these up costs upstream rate limits, not our own CPU.

groups.label: Timeouts and give-up
groups.about: When a scan stops being slow and starts being lost.

settings.label: Rescan interval, wallets in use
settings.about: A wallet somebody has open, or that belongs to an account. The real pacing knob: the queue only takes addresses that are due, so this — not scan speed — is what sets the load.
settings.note: Read by three services. The api marks a wallet stale at 3× this and reports it to the browser, so this being one value in one place is the point.

settings.label: Rescan interval, idle wallets
settings.about: Wallets that only live in anonymous portfolios nobody has opened lately. Still refreshed, just not on anyone's behalf.

settings.label: How recently a portfolio counts as in use
settings.about: Long enough that a tab left open keeps its wallets on the fast tier.

settings.label: Queue top-up interval
settings.about: How often the producer looks for addresses that have come due. Cheap — an address that is not due is simply not enqueued.

settings.label: Addresses per scanner at once
settings.about: 1 is strictly one at a time. Raising it multiplies the request rate against the same upstream sources, which is what earns a 429.

settings.label: Pause after each scan
settings.about: The pacing knob against DeBank. The scanner holds its queue slot for the whole pause, so nothing else is handed to it meanwhile.
settings.note: The scanner service has no database and cannot pick this up live; it applies there on the next deploy. The wallet service's own in-process loop reads it live.

settings.label: Parallel requests per HTTP scan
settings.about: Inside one BTC, SOL or TRON scan. Separate from prefetch, which is how many scans run at all.

settings.label: Scan claim lease
settings.about: How long an address is believed to be in flight before it counts as free again.

settings.label: When a first scan is called broken
settings.about: A wallet that has never been scanned, with no claim outstanding, waiting this long. Well past one lease on purpose — a wallet queued behind a hundred others is not a failed one.

settings.label: HTTP scan timeout
settings.about: Per request in the BTC, SOL and TRON scanners.

settings.label: EVM browser scan timeout
settings.about: A browser scan is slow by nature — a page load with chains resolving one by one.

settings.label: Alert events at once
settings.about: How many wallet-state events the alert collector works through in parallel. The work is a couple of queries.
settings.note: A consumer's prefetch is fixed when it subscribes, so this one takes effect on the next deploy of monitor-alerts.

rules.about: The lease has to outlast the slowest scan that can still come back — an EVM scan runs to its timeout and runs TWICE when it re-reads a suspicious drop, plus the pause after it. Under that and an address still being scanned gets re-enqueued, which is the whole thing the lease exists to stop.
Calling a wallet broken before its lease has even expired would say a wallet still being scanned had failed.
The slow tier being faster than the fast tier means the tiers are the wrong way round.

presets.label: Conservative
presets.about: For when the upstreams are rate-limiting us. Half the request rate, wallets refreshed a third as often.

presets.label: Aggressive
presets.about: Fresher data, more requests. Watch the 429 rate in Grafana after applying it.
